en: If opposed, he means to wreak slaughter,
To destroy the descendants of Khan Manas
Together, leaving not one alive.
He rages with renewed courage
And busies himself preparing.
He has mustered an entire army
And brought an iron-rope net.
They have all assembled together,
Saying, “I shall unleash all the strife I know;
I shall mow down the bloodthirsty Manas’s descendants
Until none remain.”
He has brought great warriors from among the giant devs
And gathered troops all along the road—
That accursed wretch himself.
Reading the trail and laying grass upon it,
He has pursued us until he has turned pale.
He heard the talk amid the clamor,
And heard that the gray wolf Manas
Still had descendants.
He heard that in broad Talas
They had established a city.
He heard that the towering gray wolf
Still had a son.
So he formed an army and gathered troops,
Mustering an immense host.
It is no ordinary darkness or night,
But the infidel’s furious demon.
He set his enmity upon us deliberately,
That scorched and rabid wretch.
Who fashioned this life with his hands
And lodged every soul upon its perch?
Is there any life wrought by human hands?
Until the whole world passes away,
Until the earth collapses and is gone,
Is there any soul that will not die?
Sarybay, son of the monster,
That insolent rabid wretch—
I shall surround him and wage war.
If my strength is enough, I shall seize him,
And carry him dangling from his horse.
If fortune favors me, I shall cast the enemy
Flat upon his back.
He was born to be my enemy;
If only the monster’s son would come,
If only my eyes might see his arrival!
To measure my spear-thrust against him
Has always been my desire—
To grapple once with that dog.
My early words have come late;
My two eyes have become four with waiting.
If I break through his flank and open a road,
If I shatter his frontier and attack,
If I crush his multitude and take spoils,
If I meet him face-to-face,
And pour out all my fury,
Clashing and fighting savagely,
May I die more bravely than all others.
May the tumult and strife I unleash increase,
May deeds like these multiply,
May my name remain as a memorial,
And may it make my renown endure.
Will my true enemy come?
This alone has filled my heart;
May the Almighty truly grant it!”
So spoke Külchoro,
Donning his bulletproof coat,
Raging and seething,
Scowling without a tremor,
Standing defiant without a murmur.
“For the united Kyrgyz people,
We shall bind our fleeting lives to a thread
And offer ourselves in sacrifice!
After calming the people and ending the turmoil,
We shall make young Seytek
A banner for these Kyrgyz,
And return rejoicing to our homes.
If the Creator grants us favor,
We shall overtake the infidel charging in arrogance
And give him his answer.
We shall behold his vaunted courage.
If calamity befalls us,
We shall see what fate has written.
If death comes from the infidel,
We shall surrender our precious lives.
If hostile death arrives, we shall die.
For our villages and our land,
For the Kyrgyz people of this country,
We shall fight seven days without rest,
Contending for our homeland.
Let us wage this struggle for the land,
So that people may say, ‘Our champions, our lions,
Sacrificed themselves for the nation,’
And their fame may remain among the people!
When the final reckoning draws near,
When hostile death makes its claim,
The tongue falls silent and cannot speak.
From this deceitful world,
What soul can flee and escape?
Will not the dug grave take everyone in—
All beneath the moon and sky,
Young rulers and old alike?
This earth crushes and devours them all.
Can one prosper by fearing death?
Has anyone lived forever in this world
With a backbone made of iron?
Champions have died, and khans have died;
This world before us is false,
And every soul whose hour comes dies.
When the water is spent and one’s days are done,
He called them to comradeship.
Speaking softly but with firm resolve,
He addressed the gray-wolf warrior:
“My heroic gray wolf, my champion,
Do you know what I know?
Do you sense what I sense?
His forefather on his father’s side—
His father was the warrior Kutu.
He was inscribed by true good fortune
As the rightful heir.
He rekindled the extinguished fire
And brought the dead soul back to life.
He joined what had been severed
And gathered what had been scattered;
He was a noble son of his father.
He bore burdens vast as a river
And was a source of life to others.
God took his father,
And after many passing years,
The inheritance came to him.
He scouted around, grieving for the land,
And went out to reconnoiter.
While on that scouting expedition,
Sarybay, son of the monster,
Appeared directly before him.
Our unyielding and faithful
Black Giant
Met him in battle,
And hostile death overtook him.
His loyal surviving comrades
Lost heart and strength,
And came fleeing in ruin.
Your true champion, the Black Giant,
Was killed by Sarybay.
Now the roaring Sarybay,
Loosing his raiders and swaggering,
Means to drive and pursue
The Kyrgyz of Ala-Too to destruction,
Allowing none of their princes to stand
And trampling us underfoot.
As though merely visiting his in-laws,
As though he were a prince ruling the people,
He grins, laughs, and rejoices.
His eighty-four kinds of armor are donned,
And his journey has taken an evil turn.
Your hero stands impatient,
His two eyes become four with watching.
The falcon son of Almambet,
Your blessed champion,
Who never bowed his neck to mortal man,
Your renowned and stubborn warrior,
Grieves at the delay.
As though going to see the bride he has won,
Your hero is upheld by fortune.
He stirs, laughs, and rejoices.
“Sarybay, son of the monster,
Has far-reaching power and potent venom;
Oh, what will become of us?” they say,
And the suffering Kyrgyz grieve.
But at the mention of death he laughs aloud:
This gray-wolf kinsman Külchoro
Stands visibly rejoicing.
In feverish haste, unable to stop,
He dons his bulletproof coat,
Arranges all his weapons,
And girds on his flashing sword.
As though a black fog were descending,
Fury spreads across his face.
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
He has thrown the whole world into turmoil.
Tall and broad-shouldered,
An unrivaled wrestler and a lion,
He never retreats before death—
Ah, what a steadfast, precious warrior!
Calling the renowned men to him,
He drew his arm behind him
And sighed as though weary.
Semetey in the encampment
Called loudly to his lion-like elder,
And to Seytek, khan of the people:
“Let us mount stallions chosen from among beasts
And drive them across every region.
Let us cast hell into their ranks
And strike them down without pause.
Let us act for the sake of our people.
Against the swine who fixed his hatred upon us,
Let us wage a fierce campaign.
Let us reach all seven divisions
And engage them in battle.
Let us search the baggage of the infidel
Who came seeking us, the warrior who ravaged the people,
Down to his very last bundle.
Let us uproot his tent poles
And unleash slaughter outright.
Let us fight to the death,
With red blood flowing,
Tearing and hacking one another apart,
Abandoning these lives and dying.
Let us go into the fray;
How can we lie grieving
Now that Sarybay has come?
We shall cast off humiliation like sheep.
If he overruns the encampment,
Warrior, it will seem that we were afraid.
Let us unleash a dreadful conflict.
Against the infidel whose strength is full,
Against the warrior who came desiring
Battle, turmoil, and devastation,
Let us march to holy war!
If hostile death arrives, let us die;
Let us test ourselves in combat.”
So spoke Külchoro,
And when the champion said these words,
They agreed, accepting them as true.
All the weak-hearted grieved,
But all the champions
Rejoiced at the word of battle.
They donned their bulletproof coats,
And girded on their finely tempered steel.
They arranged all their weapons,
Preparing to scatter the four kinds of livestock,
To bring disaster upon the people,
And to put forward without exception
Their cherished men and chiefs.
They meant to raid the ravines and seize possessions,
Burn the narrow valleys and drive off the horses,
To overtake those not yet claimed by death,
And carry away as spoils
The village beauties and widowed brides.
They fixed their hatred and prepared,
Equipping themselves with weapons.
From the desert of El-Zhürbös
And the pass of At-Baspas,
They encountered the Black Giant.
Hostile death overtook the Black Giant;
He clashed with them and was struck down,
And thus the Black Giant died.
The warriors who remained
Came fleeing in terror.
“Sarybay has slaughtered the people,” they said,
“He has brought upon us
Every strife and great conflict that accursed one knows.”
They abandoned all their possessions,
And many fled in panic.
The news had only just arrived,
And the renowned men gathered.
